summary: AstroFlame is an AI-assisted educational and analytical web platform that transforms NASA microgravity combustion data into an interactive fire-safety exploration tool. Developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge, it addresses the difficulties students and researchers face in identifying relevant combustion data, comparing experiments across conditions, and interpreting outcomes without expert knowledge. By combining predictive modeling, visual storytelling, web-based simulation, and AI-generated learning insights, the platform bridges the gap between raw scientific research and practical fire-safety understanding. It is important because it makes complex aerospace data accessible for undergraduate education and scientific exploration, helping users understand how environmental variables impact material flammability in space without needing to manually process complex datasets.
details:
What it does / How it works: AstroFlame allows users to interactively explore how environmental variables like airflow velocity, oxygen concentration, and material thickness affect flame spread rates over polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA) fuel surfaces. It includes a browser-based simulator running a TypeScript model, an analysis page featuring grouped leave-one-experiment-out cross-validation against curated NASA BASS-II and SAFFIRE-V datasets, read-only JSON data APIs, and an AI learning notes feature powered by Gemini.

Benefits & Intended Impact: The platform enhances educational accessibility for undergraduate students and teachers, aids data interpretation by providing context across different scales and experiments, and allows predictive exploration of combustion dynamics. It is intended as an evidence-bounded learning tool to foster scientific curiosity and hypothesis testing.

Tools, Languages, & Software: Developed using Next.js, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, React, and Vite on the frontend, with Python data processing scripts, Cloudflare Workers, Cloudflare Hyperdrive, and TigerData (TimescaleDB / PostgreSQL) handling the backend and database architecture. It also integrates Google Gemini for automated AI learning notes.

Creativity & Considerations: The team focused on translating dense, raw repositories from NASA's Physical Science Informatics (PSI) into a user-friendly experience by bridging rigorous statistical validation (such as grouped cross-validation) with intuitive visual feedback. Careful consideration was given to model boundaries, ensuring that predictions remain strictly tied to observed experimental ranges while explicitly marking the tool for educational research rather than certified engineering or operational safety decisions.
